source.version: arXiv:2510.26490v1 [cs.HC], 30 Oct 2025, as printed on PDF p. 1.
source.title_on_document: SCAFFOLDING CREATIVITY: HOW DIVERGENT AND CONVERGENT LLM PERSONAS SHAPE HUMAN MACHINE CREATIVE PROBLEM-SOLVING

supplement.holds: No supplement or online appendix is referenced. The PDF ends with references and contains no appendix; output statistics are in section 5.3 and Figure 6 (pp. 9–10).

paper_design_summary: Undergraduates were individually randomized to an interface offering switchable divergent and convergent personas or the same interface with baseline ChatGPT behind both buttons; both groups used AI to develop ideas for making libraries more attractive to young adults (p. 4, section 4). The paper reports 105 randomized and 101 analyzed participants, but its analyzed arm counts conflict, so the final form leaves arm-specific analyzed counts null (pp. 4-5, sections 4-5; p. 10, Figure 6). Ideas extracted from user transcripts were scored for fluency, semantic distance across participants, and semantic variation within participants during this single AI-assisted session (pp. 9-10, section 5.3; p. 12, section 6.1).

studies.label: Randomized persona-guided versus standard ChatGPT library-ideation experiment; setting not stated

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were assigned to the persona-guided interface or the baseline ChatGPT interface. Treatment participants could use both Taylor and Alex; divergent and convergent personas were not separate randomized arms. The between-condition manipulation is explicit, but the PDF does not specify laboratory supervision, online-panel delivery, or ordinary-work/coursework delivery sufficiently to select lab_rct, online_rct, or field_rct (p. 4, section 4; p. 11, section 6).
assignment.quote: Random assignment allocated 73 participants to the treatment group and 32 to the control group.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement or registry link is identified in the supplied PDF (pp. 1-16).

arms.name: Persona-guided ChatGPT (Taylor and Alex)
arms.description: Both personas were available within the same chat: Taylor used divergent-thinking prompts and temperature 0.8, while Alex used convergent-thinking prompts and temperature 0.3 (p. 4, section 4). The results text reports 69 analyzed treatment participants, whereas Figure 6 labels treatment n=70; the unambiguous arm-specific analyzed count is therefore left null (p. 5, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6).

arms.name: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
arms.description: Both buttons routed to the same baseline ChatGPT model with unmodified responses (p. 4, section 4). The results text reports 32 analyzed control participants, whereas Figure 6 labels control n=31; the unambiguous arm-specific analyzed count is therefore left null (p. 5, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6).

participants.exclusions: The paper states that four of 105 participants were excluded, but lists minimal interaction (n=1), inadequate session duration (n=2), session timeout violations (n=1), and content authenticity issues (n=1); whether reasons overlap is not explained (p. 5, section 5). The final dataset is explicitly reported as 101 conversation logs, with 69 treatment and 32 control, while Figure 6 instead labels 70 treatment and 31 control. The reported total analyzed sample is confirmed, but the arm split remains unresolved and arms[].n_analyzed is null. An additional three participants per group were excluded from survey analysis for incomplete questionnaires; those exclusions are not applied to the conversation-output sample (pp. 5-6, section 5). Fluency-specific and within-participant-distance sample counts are not printed.
participants.who: Undergraduate students from a design and engineering institution; the participant institution is not named (p. 4, section 4).
participants.quote: The final dataset comprised 101 conversation logs: 69 from the persona condition and 32 from the control condition.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4 (people randomized); pp. 5–6, section 5 (analyzed sample and exclusions); p. 10, Figure 6 (conflicting arm counts)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; the experimental chat model version is not stated. GPT-4.1 is named only for post hoc idea extraction, and text-embedding-3-large for scoring (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants freely switched between two chat buttons. Treatment prompts differentiated divergent and convergent behavior; control buttons both used unmodified baseline ChatGPT. A static system prompt, JSON conversation-state summary, and recent transcript maintained context (p. 4, section 4; p. 11, section 6). The interface also supplies ideas, as shown in Figure 1, so open_chat fits the codebook better than the content-free coach role (p. 5, Figure 1). Non-native participants were allowed to use an online Translator before submission (p. 5, section 4).

task.description: Generate ideas addressing: How can we make libraries more attractive to young adults? Ideas were extracted from the user transcripts of the human–LLM interaction (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
task.duration: 20-minute task following a five-minute interface orientation (p. 4, section 4).

outcomes.name: Between-participant semantic differentiation (paper: participant-level originality)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4.1 extracted ideas from user transcripts. Each participant's portfolio was represented by the mean-pooled centroid of normalized OpenAI text-embedding-3-large idea embeddings. The primary variant was mean cosine distance to same-condition peers, explicitly marked primary in Figure 6. The all-participant mean-distance and nearest cross-condition neighbor-distance variants are kept in this outcome rather than counted as separate outcomes. These measures compare different participants' portfolios and therefore use the codebook's diversity construct despite the paper's originality label (pp. 9–10, section 5.3; p. 10, Figure 6).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Same-condition originality: Treatment M=0.34, Control M=0.28; Welch’s t, p=2.20 × 10−6 (text); Figure 6 prints Welch p = 2.2e-06. All-participant originality: Treatment M=0.33, Control M=0.31; p=.02 (text); Figure 6 prints Welch p = 0.0215. Cross-condition nearest neighbor distance: Treatment M=0.20, Control M=0.17; p<.01 (text); Figure 6 prints Welch p = 0.00249. Figure 6 labels every comparison treatment n=70 and control n=31, conflicting with the 69/32 final-dataset split on p. 5. No numerical SD, SE, t statistic, degrees of freedom, standardized effect, or confidence-interval endpoints are reported for these contrasts. The type of plotted error bars is not defined.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, section 5.3, paragraphs beginning Three complementary originality measures and Same-condition originality; p. 10, Figure 6, exact p-value and sample labels; p. 5, section 5, conflicting sample counts

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between participant-level portfolio centroids; larger values mean greater semantic separation. The same-condition mean-distance variant is primary.
diversity_detail.computed_over: For each participant, mean cosine distance from their portfolio centroid to same-condition peers; variants use mean distance to all participants and the nearest cross-condition neighbor. Self-inclusion in the all-participant reference set is not specified. The analyzed score belongs to the participant, not to an individual idea pair (pp. 9-10, section 5.3; p. 10, Figure 6).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch tests compare participant-level distance scores; Figure 6 reports Welch p values for all three variants. Error bars are drawn, but their type and numerical endpoints are not defined in the text or caption. No adjustment for dependence induced by shared comparison portfolios is described (p. 10, section 5.3 and Figure 6).
diversity_detail.notes: The paper calls these originality measures and refers to human-LLM teams, but the analysis is explicitly participant-level. These measures compare different people's portfolios and therefore map to diversity/across_people. Larger distance means greater distinctiveness; no sign reversal is needed. The three reference-set variants are grouped as one outcome under form-spec rule 7. The arm-count conflict prevents establishing a unique analyzed arm split. The statistics_available code p_value_only describes the numerical inferential information; rounded means and p-values are printed in the prose and exact p-values are also printed in Figure 6. Unspecified graphical error bars are documented in uncertainty rather than adding figure_only.

outcomes.name: Idea fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas per participant, using a two-stage content-analysis pipeline: GPT-4.1 structured extraction from user transcripts followed by category induction. This is a count of ideas, not a count of participants; the condition comparison is participant-level (p. 9, section 5.3).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Treatment M=8.55, SD=3.85; Control M=9.23, SD=3.37. The text states no significant between-condition differences but gives no p-value or numerical test statistic for fluency. No fluency-specific arm counts are printed. The overall final-dataset counts are reported as 69 treatment and 32 control on p. 5, with a conflicting 70/31 split shown for originality in Figure 6; neither split is assumed to be the confirmed fluency sample.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, section 5.3, Computational Creativity Assessment (means, SDs, and direction); p. 5, section 5 (overall analysis counts); p. 10, Figure 6 (conflicting originality counts)

outcomes.name: Within-participant idea-portfolio variation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise semantic distance among the ideas within each participant's own portfolio, reported as within-participant idea diversity. The semantic analysis uses OpenAI text-embedding-3-large. Coded flexibility because this measures variation within a person's ideas, not diversity across different people (pp. 9–10, section 5.3).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Mean pairwise distance: Treatment M=0.59, Control M=0.59, p=.90. No numerical SD, SE, test statistic, confidence interval, or outcome-specific sample counts are printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Within-participant idea diversity

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Individuals were explicitly randomly assigned to persona-guided or baseline ChatGPT for the library-ideation task, an ai_design comparison between generative-AI configurations (p. 4, section 4). The paper reports 105 randomized people and a final analyzed dataset of 101 participant conversation logs (p. 5, section 5). Figure 6 also represents 101 analyzed people, with treatment n=70 and control n=31, although the results text gives 69 and 32; the conflicting analyzed arm counts remain null and do not unsettle the total above 50 (p. 10, Figure 6). Fluency and semantic-distance scores are computed from ideas extracted from participants' user transcripts, meeting the output-scoring criterion (pp. 9-10, section 5.3). These are immediate outputs produced with AI available; autonomous rounds appear only as future work (p. 4, section 4; p. 12, sections 6.1-6.2). The exclusion-reason discrepancy, unresolved RCT setting, unspecified participant-facing model version and full prompts, and unspecified Figure 6 uncertainty affect extraction or replication but no eligibility criterion. The inconsistent control n in the separate question-asking analysis is not used as a count of unique people (p. 8, section 5.2).

one_line_finding: Persona-guided ChatGPT increased between-person semantic distance versus standard ChatGPT (M=0.34 vs 0.28; p=2.20 × 10−6), with no significant fluency difference (M=8.55 vs 9.23) or within-person distance difference (M=0.59 vs 0.59; p=.90; pp. 9-10, section 5.3 and Figure 6).
open_questions: Which analyzed arm counts are correct: 69 treatment/32 control in the results text or 70/31 on every Figure 6 comparison? Confirm outcome-specific counts for fluency and within-participant distance as well (p. 5, section 5; pp. 9-10, section 5.3 and Figure 6).
The paper states four exclusions but lists reason counts of 1, 2, 1, and 1. Were reasons overlapping, or is a count incorrect (p. 5, section 5)?
Was the randomized session supervised in a laboratory, administered remotely, or part of ordinary coursework? The RCT setting is not stated sufficiently to select a subtype (pp. 4-5, section 4).
Which ChatGPT model/version and complete persona prompts were used for participant-facing chat? GPT-4.1 is named only for later idea extraction (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
What do the Figure 6 error bars represent, and what numerical participant-level SDs, SEs, or interval bounds underlie the distance comparisons (p. 10, section 5.3 and Figure 6)?

What observations do the behavioral-analysis counts represent: treatment/control n=63/51 for divergent interactions and 59/51 for convergent interactions, despite only 32 controls being randomized? Clarify the unit or correct the counts; these process-analysis counts are not used for the creativity-output sample (p. 8, section 5.2; p. 4, section 4).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from two present, parseable raw forms. Read the complete 470-line markdown conversion through the final references; the supplied PDF contains 16 pages and no appendix or embedded supplement. Independently checked PDF text for version, assignment, sample, task, exclusions, and every retained numerical output statistic; inspected embedded Figures 1 and 6 directly in memory. No external lookup was needed. No effect sizes or uncertainties were calculated, and no values were estimated from bar heights. The substantive A/B differences are B's additional translator provision, B's figure_only statistics flag, and the different result coverage in the one-line findings. The final form retains the translator provision and both summaries' supported result details; it uses p_value_only for the between-person outcome because numerical means and p-values are printed, while the undefined graphical error bars are described separately. Other differences in wording, arm/outcome labels, page-range specificity, and the placement of already-shared information are not counted as substantive disagreements. Both forms contain the same three output outcomes and the same reported numeric results. Agreement checks retain the confirmed total of 101 analyzed people but do not confirm a unique arm split; both final arm counts are null, with both source-reported splits preserved in descriptions and statistics. The exclusion-reason discrepancy is also unresolved in the source. n_unresolved counts unresolved A/B differences only; the shared source limitations remain in open_questions and the unconfirmed agreement checks. The RCT subtype, participant-facing model/version, full persona prompts, and Figure 6 uncertainty remain unspecified. The participant country is not inferred from author affiliations. The arm_means_sds_ns flag for fluency denotes printed means and SDs plus reported overall sample counts; it does not establish complete or unambiguous outcome-specific arm Ns. The three between-participant distance definitions are retained as variants of one outcome. Within-participant semantic variation is flexibility, not across-person diversity. Table 1 and Figures 2-4 concern subjective creativity/helpfulness, ownership, persona preferences, AI proficiency, and personality associations; these are not output-scored creativity measures. Sections 5.1-5.2 and Figure 5 concern interaction and question-asking processes and are excluded. Section 5.3 discusses category-based flexibility and elaboration generically but reports no separate comparisons for them. The incentive for a highest-rated submission has no reported judged-output comparison. Exploratory associations among the already-listed outcomes and persona preferences do not add randomized contrasts. No shared sample, preregistration, company participation, data/code repository, or supplementary material is identified in the document. Use of OpenAI tools is not treated as evidence of company involvement. All scored outputs arose during AI interaction; autonomous rounds are proposed as future work, not reported as an after-AI phase. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading all 470 markdown lines through the final references, checking the relevant PDF text, and inspecting all six embedded figures directly in memory. The supplied PDF has 16 pages, no appendix, and no embedded files; no supplement, posted data, or code is identified. Assignment, outcome, and people challenge files all contain empty problems arrays, so final.challenge_resolution is empty and n_corrected, n_rejected, and n_open are all zero. All reported output statistics and Figure 6 labels were confirmed. Counts after exclusions are described as analyzed. The additional behavioral-count inconsistency noted in the people check was confirmed on p. 8, section 5.2: divergent treatment/control n=63/51 and convergent n=59/51, versus 32 controls randomized on p. 4, section 4. These are process analyses, not additional human samples or creativity-output contrasts. Every open question has an eligibility assessment and a resolution source in final.open_items; none affects eligibility. All reconciliation.differences were already resolved, and the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged, including the two unconfirmed agreement checks covered by the sample-count and exclusion open items. The original experimental design is not a reanalysis of another paper. No external lookup, derived effect size, or graphical estimate was used.

differences.a: Participants freely switched between two chat buttons. Treatment prompts differentiated divergent and convergent behavior; control buttons both used unmodified baseline ChatGPT. A static system prompt, JSON conversation-state summary, and recent transcript maintained context. Although the authors call the interface coach-like, it also supplies content, as shown in Figure 1, so it does not meet the codebook's content-free coach definition (pp. 4–5, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 11, section 6).
differences.b: Participants entered messages and freely chose between persona buttons throughout ideation. Treatment combined divergent and convergent prompt configurations; control used baseline ChatGPT behind both buttons (p. 4, section 4; p. 11, section 6). Although described as coach-like, the interface supplies substantive suggestions as well as questions, as shown in Figure 1 (p. 5), so it does not meet the codebook's content-free coach definition. Non-native participants could also use an online translator before submission (p. 5, section 4).
differences.resolved: Participants freely switched between two chat buttons. Treatment prompts differentiated divergent and convergent behavior; control buttons both used unmodified baseline ChatGPT. A static system prompt, JSON conversation-state summary, and recent transcript maintained context (p. 4, section 4; p. 11, section 6). The interface also supplies ideas, as shown in Figure 1, so open_chat fits the codebook better than the content-free coach role (p. 5, Figure 1). Non-native participants were allowed to use an online Translator before submission (p. 5, section 4).

The authors need to identify overlapping exclusion reasons or correct the reported counts.
